newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices extend gains, while orange juice falls.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices extend gains, while orange juice falls.

text.p: Coffee prices rose to a 21-month high Thursday on concerns about tight supplies in South America and possible shipping problems in strikebound Colombia.

Frozen concentrated orange juice prices bounced back after falling to four-year lows on Wednesday. Wheat edged higher as traders expect increased exports soon because Australia and Canada may be unable to compete.
Coffee futures at New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange surged for the sixth straight session, with contract highs set for most contracts.
March coffee ended up 8.20 cents at 180.05 cents a pound, its highest close in 21 months. It peaked earlier in the session at 181.00 cents.
The surge in coffee prompted leading U.S. brands Maxwell House and Folgers to increase supermarket prices by 15 cents on their 13-ounce cans, effective next month.
Maxwell House announced its increase, which raises the price of a standard can to $2.41, Thursday following Folgers' announcement Tuesday.

"It is a strong market and it is important to remember it began taking off in early January," said Prudential Securities analyst Arthur Stevenson. "Nothing fresh fundamentally happened today, but basically the market remains focused on the supply situation."
The situation includes forecasts for smaller crops this year from top producers Brazil and No. 2 Colombia and concerns a nationwide strike by government workers in Colombia will slow exports.
"The (Colombia) strike is not interfering with the normal flow of coffee," he said, "But I think people are concerned it might expand to other sectors."

Also bullish was news the Association of Producing Countries plans to go ahead with export quota cuts in the first half of 1997, and news of depleted inventories in both producing and consuming countries.
At the New York Cotton Exchange, frozen concentrated futures closed higher in a technical correction to Wednesday's losses, traders said.

On Wednesday, prices fell to four-year lows after the Agriculture Department left unchanged its estimate of the Florida crop at a record 220 million 90-pound boxes. Belying market expectations, the department increased yields to 1.54 gallons of orange juice a box from 1.53 gallons.

Analysts warned supply and demand news for orange juice remained bearish. High retail prices have dampened demand for orange juice and abundant supplies are projected for Brazil, they said. Also, a cold spell forecast for Florida's citrus belt this weekend is not expected to damage the crop.
March frozen concentrated orange juice futures closed 2.35 cent higher at 76.90 cents a pound.

Soft red winter wheat futures at the Chicago Board of Trade closed higher on prospects for a 450,000-metric ton sale of U.S. wheat to Pakistan and on news Japan this week bought 120,000 tons of U.S. wheat.

Transportation problems in Canada prompted speculation that Asian buyers will turn to U.S. wheat, and news that Australian wheat sales are fully booked fuelled hopes their wheat customers would turn to the United States.
CBOT March wheat rose 1-3/4 cents to $3.59 per bushel.
New York Mercantile Exchange oil prices ended mixed as traders sold heating oil to buy gasoline and crude amid slackening demand for heating oil and diesel fuel in Gulf of Mexico cash markets.
NYMEX March heating oil settled 0.93 cent lower at 59.92 cents a gallon. March crude ended at $22.02, up 16 cents a barrel while March gasoline finished up 0.29 cent at 63.18 cents a gallon.
